content: 1. Household members and close contacts of individuals with tuberculosis (TB) who exhibit symptoms consistent with TB disease may be offered counseling and testing for HIV as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence. 2. All household contacts of an index case who is a person living with HIV should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation, despite very low certainty of evidence. 3. The prevention of TB in children and adolescents includes consolidated recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on TB infection, prevention, and control, as well as guidance on Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination and tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT). These recommendations are derived from WHO's 2019 update on TB infection prevention and control, the WHO position paper on BCG vaccines, and the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. 4. Administrative controls, such as triaging individuals with TB symptoms or disease, are recommended to reduce Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission to healthcare workers, community health workers, and others in high-risk settings. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 5. Respiratory separation or isolation of individuals with presumed or confirmed infectious TB is recommended to reduce transmission to healthcare workers and others in healthcare facilities. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 6. Prompt initiation of effective TB treatment for individuals with TB disease is strongly recommended to reduce transmission to healthcare workers, individuals attending healthcare facilities, and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 7. Respiratory hygiene, including cough etiquette, is strongly recommended for individuals with presumed or confirmed TB to reduce transmission to healthcare workers and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation has low certainty in the estimates of effects. 8. Environmental controls, such as upper-room germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) systems, are conditionally recommended to reduce TB transmission in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on moderate certainty in the estimates of effects. 9. Ventilation systems, including natural, mixed-mode, mechanical ventilation, and recirculated air through high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, are conditionally recommended to reduce TB transmission in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 10. Particulate respirators, used within a respiratory protection program, are conditionally recommended to reduce TB transmission to healthcare workers and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 11. In countries with high TB and/or leprosy incidence, a single dose of BCG vaccine should be administered to neonates at birth or as soon as possible thereafter to prevent TB and leprosy. If the birth dose is missed, catch-up vaccination is recommended at the earliest opportunity. Co-administration of BCG with the hepatitis B birth dose is safe and strongly recommended. 12. In countries with low TB incidence, selective BCG vaccination may be considered for neonates in recognized high-risk groups, such as those with close contacts who have a history of TB or leprosy or those in households with connections to high-incidence countries. 13. Revaccination with BCG is not recommended, as studies show minimal or no additional benefit against TB or leprosy. The absence of a BCG scar after vaccination does not indicate a lack of protection and is not a reason for revaccination. 14. HIV-infected children vaccinated with BCG at birth are at increased risk of disseminated BCG disease. However, if they are receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), are clinically well, and immunologically stable (CD4% > 25% for children under 5 years or CD4 count ≥ 200 for those over 5 years), they should be vaccinated with BCG. 15. In populations with high HIV prevalence and TB burden, the benefits of preventing severe TB through BCG vaccination at birth outweigh the risks. Neonates born to women of unknown HIV status should be vaccinated. For neonates of HIV-infected women, vaccination should proceed if there is no clinical evidence of HIV infection, regardless of maternal ART status. 16. For neonates with confirmed HIV infection, BCG vaccination should be delayed until ART has been initiated and the infant is clinically and immunologically stable (CD4% > 25%). 17. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of ART status, pregnancy, or previous TB treatment history. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty in the estimates of effects. 18. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who are in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty in the estimates of effects. 19. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of TB contact history. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty in the estimates of effects. 20. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed TB treatment may receive TB preventive treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty in the estimates of effects. 21. Children under 5 years who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment, even if TB infection testing is unavailable. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty in the estimates of effects. 22. In selected high-risk household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB, preventive treatment may be considered based on individualized risk assessment and sound clinical justification. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 23. Systematic TB infection testing and treatment are recommended for individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or with silicosis. This is a strong recommendation with low to very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 24. Systematic TB infection testing and treatment may be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. This is a conditional recommendation with low to very low certainty in the estimates of effects. 25. Systematic TB infection testing and treatment are not recommended for individuals with diabetes, those who engage in harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups. 26. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have TB disease and should be offered preventive treatment. 27. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who report symptoms of TB should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If TB disease is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. 28. Chest radiography may be offered to individuals living with HIV on ART, and preventive treatment should be given to those with no abnormal radiographic findings. 29. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or cough, or have a history of contact with a person with TB, should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If TB disease is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. 30. Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for TB infection. 31. Recommended TB preventive treatment options include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative options include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. 32. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive TB infection test and are unlikely to have TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of ART status, immunosuppression level, pregnancy, or previous TB treatment history.
